cards.title: Concurrency Control — The Serialisability Goal
cards.teaser: Many transactions run at the same time on the same data. The engine's job is to make the result look as if they ran one at a time — the serialisability goal — without paying the full price of actually running them serially.

runs.text: A database that processes one transaction at a time is trivially correct but useless under load. Concurrency is a performance necessity. The problem is that concurrent access creates interleaving: transaction T1 reads a row, transaction T2 writes it, T1 reads it again. Now T1 has seen two different values for the same row within a single transaction. That is wrong.
The standard correctness criterion for concurrent transaction processing is
serializability
: a concurrent execution of a set of transactions is correct if its result is equivalent to
some
serial execution of those same transactions. The engine does not have to run them one at a time; it just has to produce an outcome that
could have
come from running them one at a time.
Why is this hard? Three fundamental conflict types drive all anomalies:

items.text: Read-Write (rw).
T1 reads a row that T2 then writes (non-repeatable read).
Write-Read (wr).
T1 writes a row that T2 then reads (dirty read).
Write-Write (ww).
T1 and T2 both write the same row; the last write wins, erasing the first (lost update).

runs.text: Concurrency control mechanisms — locks, version chains, validation protocols — all exist to prevent dangerous interleavings of these three conflict types. The theoretical foundation is Adya's 1999 formalization of isolation, which describes anomalies in terms of cycles in a dependency graph rather than the implementation-specific lock-based criteria of SQL-92.

The SQL-92 standard defined isolation in terms of observable anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads). Adya (1999) showed this definition is incomplete and ambiguous. His generalized formalization — defining isolation levels via forbidden cycle patterns in a serialization graph — is the theoretical basis on which modern systems like SSI are built.

When many transactions run at the same time, their reads and writes can interleave in ways that produce wrong answers — like reading a value that someone else is still changing. Concurrency control exists to ensure the outcome looks as if the transactions ran one at a time, even though they actually ran together.

cards.title: Pessimistic vs Optimistic Concurrency
cards.teaser: Lock-and-block says: assume conflict is likely, so acquire locks before touching data. Optimistic says: assume conflict is rare, so run freely and validate at commit — aborting if a conflict is discovered. The right choice depends on contention.

runs.text: Concurrency control strategies split into two philosophical camps:

items.text: Pessimistic (locking).

Before accessing a data item, a transaction acquires a lock. If the lock is held by a conflicting transaction, the newcomer blocks. No work is wasted — a transaction only proceeds when it has the right to do so. Cost: blocking, deadlock risk, and lock manager overhead even when conflicts are rare.
Optimistic (OCC).

Transactions read and write freely using private workspace. At commit time, the engine validates whether any of the reads or writes conflict with other committed transactions. If no conflict, commit. If conflict, abort and retry. Cost: aborted work, but no blocking and no lock overhead during execution.

runs.text: Optimistic concurrency (Kung and Robinson, 1981) thrives when conflicts are rare — read-heavy OLAP workloads, or short transactions in low-contention domains. It degrades badly under high write contention: a transaction may execute for seconds, validate, fail, and repeat the whole cycle. Pessimistic locking thrives under high contention because contenders queue rather than retry.

Modern engines rarely use pure OCC. Instead, they layer optimism on top of MVCC: transactions read old versions freely (no read locks needed) while writes acquire locks. This hybrid — used by PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle, and SQL Server in snapshot mode — gets the best of both worlds: non-blocking reads and orderly write serialization.

PostgreSQL's SSI mode (pg 9.1+) is the clearest production example of optimistic serialization: it tracks read-write dependencies at runtime and aborts only the minimum set of transactions necessary to break a dangerous cycle. The happy path — no conflicts — has near-zero overhead.

Pessimistic concurrency locks data before touching it — block if someone else has it. Optimistic runs freely and checks for conflicts only at commit time — if there is a conflict, redo the work. Locking is better when conflicts are frequent; optimistic is better when they are rare.

cards.title: Isolation Levels — The Spectrum
cards.teaser: The SQL standard defines four isolation levels as a cost-vs-correctness dial: from Read Uncommitted (fastest, most anomalies) to Serialisable (correct, most overhead). Real engines add a fifth level — Snapshot Isolation — between Repeatable Read and Serialisable.

runs.text: SQL-92 codified four isolation levels, each allowing a different subset of anomalies. In practice, most engines extend this with Snapshot Isolation (SI), which sits between Repeatable Read and Serialisable on the correctness axis:

explanation.text:
Level                  | Dirty Read | Non-repeatable Read | Phantom Read | Write Skew
-----------------------+------------+---------------------+--------------+-----------
Read Uncommitted       |    YES     |        YES          |     YES      |    YES
Read Committed         |     no     |        YES          |     YES      |    YES
Repeatable Read        |     no     |         no          |     YES      |    YES
Snapshot Isolation     |     no     |         no          |      no*     |    YES
Serializable (S2PL/SSI)|     no     |         no          |      no      |     no

* SI prevents phantoms caused by the same predicate re-scan, but write skew is
  a different class of anomaly (see card 5).

items.text: Read Uncommitted.

A transaction can read rows written by uncommitted transactions. Allowed only in bulk analytics where approximate answers are acceptable (e.g., reporting dashboards). Almost no production OLTP workload uses this.
Read Committed.
The default in PostgreSQL and Oracle. Reads see only committed data, but repeated reads of the same row within a transaction may return different values.
Repeatable Read.

The default in MySQL InnoDB. Once a row is read, subsequent reads in the same transaction see the same version. Phantoms (new rows matching a predicate) are still possible under a locking implementation — InnoDB uses gap locks to prevent them.
Snapshot Isolation.

Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot taken at its start (or at its first read, depending on the engine). Oracle calls this "read consistency". PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read is actually SI. Not in SQL-92 but offered by every major RDBMS.
Serialisable.
The strongest guarantee. Implemented via S2PL (predicate locks) or SSI. SQL Server's default when using the SERIALIZABLE isolation hint; PostgreSQL offers it via SSI.

runs.text: Isolation level is a dial between performance and correctness. The lower the level, the more anomalies you allow in exchange for less blocking. Read Committed is the most common default — you see only committed data but the same row can look different if you read it twice. Serialisable guarantees perfectly consistent results but costs more.

cards.title: Dirty Reads — The Bug at Read Uncommitted
cards.teaser: A dirty read occurs when one transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed. The reader may act on data that will be rolled back — a fundamental consistency violation that Read Committed prevents by design.

runs.text: Consider a bank transfer: T1 debits account A by $100 and credits account B by $100. Between the two writes, T2 reads both balances. At Read Uncommitted, T2 sees the debit but not yet the credit — the total money in the system appears to have decreased by $100. If T1 then aborts, those writes are rolled back; T2's read was based on data that never existed.
Read Committed eliminates dirty reads by ensuring that a reader always sees the
latest committed version

of a row. In a lock-based implementation, this is achieved by releasing read locks immediately after the read (rather than holding them until commit). In an MVCC implementation, the reader simply ignores versions with an uncommitted transaction ID — it always selects the most recently committed version.

PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle, and SQL Server all default to Read Committed or higher. Read Uncommitted is rarely used outside of approximate-counting or reporting scenarios where absolute consistency is not required and blocking is unacceptable.

MySQL InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ. PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED. Oracle does not implement READ UNCOMMITTED at all — the minimum level is READ COMMITTED, where MVCC makes dirty reads structurally impossible.

A dirty read is reading someone else's uncommitted work. If they abort, you built decisions on data that was never real. Read Committed eliminates this by only letting you see committed rows — either by holding short read locks or by MVCC skipping uncommitted versions.

cards.title: Write Skew and Phantom Reads — What Snapshot Isolation Misses
cards.teaser: Snapshot Isolation prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and most phantoms — but it does not prevent write skew or the booking anomaly. These are the bugs that require true Serialisable isolation to eliminate.

runs.text: Write skew
is the classic anomaly that exposes SI's blind spot. The canonical example is the on-call doctor problem (Berenson et al., 1995):
This is write skew: two transactions each read a shared state, make a decision based on that state, and update
disjoint
rows. Because they write different rows, SI sees no write-write conflict and lets both commit. The result violates an invariant that neither transaction individually broke.
Phantom reads
are a related concern. A phantom occurs when T1 executes a predicate scan (e.g.,
SELECT ... WHERE salary > 100000

), T2 inserts a new row that matches the predicate and commits, and T1 re-executes the same scan to find a new row. Under Repeatable Read with row locks, T1 holds locks on existing rows but not on the gap where new rows could be inserted. MySQL InnoDB uses
gap locks
and
next-key locks
to prevent this even at Repeatable Read.
Write skew requires Serialisable isolation (via predicate locks in S2PL or rw-dependency tracking in SSI) to prevent. It cannot be fixed by locking rows that were read — the fix requires locking the
predicate
itself.

Write skew: two transactions each check a shared condition, see it pass, and each update a different row — so there is no write conflict. But together, their updates violate the condition that both checked. Snapshot Isolation cannot catch this because it only prevents conflicting writes to the same row. Fixing write skew requires Serialisable isolation.

cards.title: Two-Phase Locking — The Growing and Shrinking Phases
cards.teaser: 2PL is the textbook locking protocol that guarantees serialisability: a transaction may acquire locks at any time but may not acquire any new lock once it has released one. This creates two phases — growing and shrinking — and a proof that no cycle can form in the serialisation graph.

runs.text: Two-Phase Locking (2PL) was first described formally in the paper that defined the modern transaction model (Eswaran, Gray, Lorie, Traiger, 1976). The protocol is simple: during the
growing phase
a transaction may acquire locks but not release any. Once it releases its first lock, it enters the
shrinking phase
and may no longer acquire new locks.

explanation.text:
Time →

  T1:  [acquire S(A)]--[acquire X(B)]--[release S(A)]--[release X(B)]
                          ↑                ↑
                    Growing phase     Shrinking phase starts here

  2PL rule: no new lock may be acquired after the first release.

  Violation of 2PL:
  T1:  [acquire S(A)]--[release S(A)]--[acquire X(B)]  ← ILLEGAL
                               ↑ releasing before all acquires done

runs.text: Why does 2PL guarantee serializability? Informally: if T1 holds a lock that T2 is waiting for, T2 cannot commit before T1 releases it. Because T1 cannot then acquire new locks (it is in shrinking phase), the lock-point ordering of transactions forms a valid serial order. A formal proof shows that 2PL execution graphs are acyclic.
The weakness of basic 2PL: if T1 releases a lock during its shrinking phase and T2 acquires that lock and commits, T2 has seen T1's partial work. If T1 later aborts, T2 may have performed a
cascading abort
— T2 must be rolled back because it read dirty data. This is exactly what Strict 2PL fixes.

The theoretical result is that 2PL is both necessary and sufficient for conflict-serializability in a system that only uses locking: any schedule produced by 2PL is serializable, and any serializable schedule can be produced by some 2PL execution (Gray, Lorie, Putzolu, Traiger, 1976).

2PL says: you can acquire locks freely, but the moment you release one, you cannot acquire any more. This creates a point of no return — the lock point — after which the transaction is committed to its current lock set. The ordering of lock points across transactions defines a legal serial order, which is why 2PL guarantees serializability.

cards.title: Strict 2PL — Hold All Locks Until Commit
cards.teaser: Strict 2PL (S2PL) tightens the rule: hold every write lock until the transaction commits or aborts. This eliminates cascading aborts — no other transaction can read dirty data because the dirty data is locked until the outcome is known.

runs.text: Basic 2PL allows locks to be released during the shrinking phase, while the transaction is still running. This creates a window where another transaction can read uncommitted data, leading to cascading aborts: if T1 aborts, every transaction that read T1's dirty data must also abort.
Strict 2PL closes this window: all
exclusive (write) locks
are held until the transaction commits or aborts. The transaction can release shared (read) locks earlier, but write locks are pinned to the transaction's lifetime.

explanation.text:
Basic 2PL             Strict 2PL (S2PL)

  T1:  [acquire X(A)]...[release X(A)]...COMMIT
         ←lock held→                            ← X(A) held until COMMIT

  T2 waiting for X(A):  
         ↓ (blocked)           ↓ (unblocked after T1 COMMIT)
        ...                   T2 runs after T1 has definitively committed

With S2PL, T2 can never read T1's uncommitted writes.
With basic 2PL, T1 could release X(A) before COMMIT, letting T2 read dirty data.

runs.text: Strong Strict 2PL (SS2PL, also called Rigorous 2PL) goes further:
all

locks (shared and exclusive) are held until commit. This is the variant actually implemented in most commercial RDBMSs: SQL Server uses SS2PL under SERIALIZABLE isolation, and it was the traditional mode for IBM DB2. SS2PL makes lock release atomic with commit, simplifying recovery: the lock manager can use commit order as the serialization order.

The cost of S2PL is concurrency. A long-running transaction holding write locks on hot rows blocks every other writer for its entire duration. This is the primary motivation for MVCC: readers never block writers, and writers never block readers.

Strict 2PL says: hold all write locks until you commit or abort — never release them early. This means no one can read your uncommitted changes, so no cascading aborts are possible. The downside is that a slow transaction holds locks on hot rows for its entire lifetime, blocking everyone else.

cards.title: Lock Manager Internals — Tables, Queues, and Modes
cards.teaser: The lock manager is the engine subsystem that tracks which transactions hold which locks and which are waiting. At its core: a hash table keyed by resource ID, where each bucket holds a granted set and a wait queue.

runs.text: The lock manager maintains a
lock table
: a hash map from
resource identifier
(table OID + page number + slot number, or just table OID for table-level locks) to a
lock entry
. Each lock entry contains:

items.text: Granted set.
The list of (transaction ID, lock mode) pairs that currently hold the lock.
Wait queue.
An ordered list of (transaction ID, lock mode, condition variable) for transactions that are blocked waiting for the lock.
Group mode.
The effective mode of the granted set (the strongest mode currently held), used for fast compatibility checks.

explanation.text:
Lock Table (simplified):

  Resource: row (page=42, slot=7)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Granted: [(T1, S), (T3, S)]   group_mode = S         │
  │ Waiting: [(T2, X, cv2), (T4, S, cv4)]                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  T2 wants X — incompatible with S in granted set → blocked
  T4 wants S — compatible with S, but T2 is already waiting:
    → FIFO: T4 must wait behind T2 to prevent starvation

On T1 and T3 releasing:
  → T2's X lock is granted (granted set now empty before it runs)
  → T2 wakes via condition variable cv2
  → T4 remains queued until T2 releases

runs.text: PostgreSQL's lock manager lives in shared memory at
src/backend/storage/lmgr/
. It uses a partitioned hash table (128 partitions by default,
NUM_LOCK_PARTITIONS

) to reduce contention on the lock table itself. Each partition has its own LWLock (lightweight lock). SQL Server uses a similar partitioned lock table stored in buffer pool memory, with escalation to coarser granularity under memory pressure.

The lock manager is a hash table. The key is the resource being locked. The value is the list of who holds it and the queue of who is waiting. When a transaction wants a lock, the manager checks compatibility with current holders. If compatible, grant it. If not, add to the wait queue and put the transaction to sleep.

cards.title: Lock Granularity — Rows, Pages, and Tables
cards.teaser: Locks can be acquired at row level, page level, or table level. Finer granularity means more concurrency but higher lock manager overhead. Coarser granularity reduces overhead but serialises more work. Gray (1976) formalized the granularity hierarchy and the intent lock protocol that makes it manageable.

runs.text: Jim Gray's 1976 paper "Granularity of Locks and Degrees of Consistency in a Shared Data Base" identified the fundamental trade-off: each lock acquired has overhead (hash lookup, memory, wait-queue manipulation). A transaction that updates one million rows will acquire one million row locks — cheaper per lock than a full table scan with a single table lock, but one million times the lock overhead.

explanation.text:
Lock granularity hierarchy:

  Database
    └── Table (or relation)
          └── Page (typically 8KB)
                └── Row (tuple)

Trade-off:

  Granularity  │ Concurrency   │ Lock overhead  │ Use case
  ─────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────┼─────────────────────
  Table        │ Low           │ 1 lock         │ DDL, bulk import
  Page         │ Medium        │ N/pagesize     │ Rare in modern DBs
  Row          │ High          │ 1 per row      │ OLTP default

Lock escalation (SQL Server, DB2):
  When a transaction acquires > 5,000 row locks on the same table,
  the engine may escalate to a table lock to reclaim memory.

runs.text: PostgreSQL uses row-level locks exclusively for DML (data manipulation), and table-level locks for DDL. It does
not

escalate row locks to table locks — because MVCC makes row-level read locks unnecessary, lock counts remain manageable. SQL Server and DB2 both support lock escalation as a memory-management mechanism.

MySQL InnoDB uses row-level locks implemented as index record locks. Because InnoDB locks index entries (not the rows themselves), a table without an index is effectively table-locked for writes — every DML operation must scan the full clustered index, locking all entries. This is why every InnoDB table should have a primary key.

Locking finer-grained resources (rows instead of tables) means more transactions can run at the same time — but each lock costs memory and CPU. A bulk operation updating a million rows might be better served by one table lock than a million row locks. Modern OLTP engines default to row-level locks and escalate to table locks only when under memory pressure.

cards.title: Lock Modes — S, X, IS, IX, and the Compatibility Matrix
cards.teaser: Shared locks allow concurrent readers. Exclusive locks block everyone. Intent locks (IS, IX) mark the path from coarse-grained locks to fine-grained ones, letting the engine check table-level compatibility without scanning every row lock beneath it.

runs.text: Gray (1976) defined the standard lock mode hierarchy. The five core modes:

items.text: S (Shared).
Read lock. Multiple transactions may hold S locks on the same resource simultaneously.
X (Exclusive).
Write lock. Only one transaction may hold X; incompatible with S and other X locks.
IS (Intent Shared).
Placed on an ancestor (e.g., table) to signal that S locks are held on descendant rows. Allows other IS and IX holders at the table level.
IX (Intent Exclusive).
Placed on an ancestor to signal X locks are held on descendant rows. Allows other IS and IX holders but blocks table-level S.
SIX (Shared + Intent Exclusive).
Holds a table-level S lock (read the whole table) while also holding row-level X locks (update some rows). Used for statements like UPDATE with a full-table scan.

explanation.text:
Compatibility matrix (Y = compatible, N = conflict):

  Requested →
  Held ↓    │  IS  │  IX  │  S   │  SIX │  X
  ──────────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────
  IS        │  Y   │  Y   │  Y   │  Y   │  N
  IX        │  Y   │  Y   │  N   │  N   │  N
  S         │  Y   │  N   │  Y   │  N   │  N
  SIX       │  Y   │  N   │  N   │  N   │  N
  X         │  N   │  N   │  N   │  N   │  N

Example: T1 holds IX on the table (is updating rows inside).
  → T2 wants S on the table (full table read) → CONFLICT (IX vs S = N)
  → T3 wants IS on the table (row-level reads) → OK (IX vs IS = Y)

runs.text: Intent locks are the key to efficient multi-level locking. Without them, the engine would need to scan all row locks under a table to decide whether a table-level lock is safe. With intent locks, a single compatibility check at the table level is sufficient — intent locks propagate the "something is locked below" signal upward.

S locks allow concurrent readers; X locks give exclusive write access. Intent locks (IS, IX) are placed on parent nodes in the hierarchy to signal what is happening lower down. Instead of scanning all child locks, the manager just checks the intent lock on the parent. This makes multi-level locking efficient.

cards.title: Deadlock Detection — Wait-For Graphs and Cycle Detection
cards.teaser: A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions are each waiting for a lock held by another in the cycle. Engines detect deadlocks by periodically constructing a wait-for graph and running cycle detection — then aborting the cheapest transaction to break the cycle.

runs.text: Deadlock is a natural consequence of mutual exclusion and blocking. Once deadlock is possible, the engine must either prevent it (deadlock avoidance) or detect and resolve it (deadlock detection). Most production systems use detection because avoidance requires ordering resources or timestamp-based protocols that hurt throughput.

explanation.text:
Wait-For Graph:

  T1 holds X(A), wants X(B)
  T2 holds X(B), wants X(A)

  Graph nodes:  T1, T2
  Graph edges:  T1 → T2  (T1 waits for T2 to release B)
                T2 → T1  (T2 waits for T1 to release A)

  Cycle: T1 → T2 → T1  → DEADLOCK

  Three-way deadlock:
  T1 → T2 → T3 → T1  → cycle of length 3

  Resolution: pick victim (T3 — fewest locks held / lowest cost),
              abort T3, T1 and T2 can proceed.

runs.text: PostgreSQL runs deadlock detection in the background: when a lock request blocks for more than
deadlock_timeout

(default 1 second), the engine triggers a deadlock check for that waiter. This lazy approach avoids the overhead of maintaining a live global wait-for graph — deadlock detection only runs when a transaction has been waiting long enough to warrant the check.
SQL Server uses a dedicated
lock monitor thread

that wakes every 5 seconds (or sooner if a chain of blocked transactions is detected) and scans the wait-for graph. The victim is chosen to minimise rollback cost: typically the transaction with the least accumulated log records.

Applications should be written to handle deadlock errors gracefully. In PostgreSQL, a deadlock raises error code 40P01; in SQL Server, error 1205. The correct response is to catch the error, wait briefly, and retry the entire transaction from scratch.

A deadlock is a cycle of waiting: T1 waits for T2, T2 waits for T1, neither can proceed. The engine detects this by building a wait-for graph and looking for cycles. When it finds one, it picks the cheapest transaction to kill, aborts it, and lets the others proceed. The killed transaction gets an error and should retry.

cards.title: Deadlock Avoidance — Wound-Wait and Wait-Die
cards.teaser: Deadlock avoidance prevents cycles from forming in the first place by assigning timestamps to transactions and using them to decide who blocks and who aborts when a conflict arises. Two protocols — wound-wait and wait-die — each make a different tradeoff.

runs.text: Timestamp-based avoidance assigns each transaction a
timestamp
at start time. When T_i requests a lock held by T_j, the relative age determines the outcome. Both protocols were formalized by Rosenkrantz, Stearns, and Lewis (1978).

items.text: Wait-Die (non-preemptive).

If T_i is older than T_j (i.e., T_i.ts < T_j.ts), T_i waits. If T_i is younger, T_i dies (aborts and retries). Old transactions always wait; young transactions always die. Direction: younger → older = wait; younger → older conflict = die.
Wound-Wait (preemptive).
If T_i is older than T_j, T_i wounds T_j (forces T_j to abort). If T_i is younger, T_i waits. Old transactions preempt young ones; young transactions always wait for old ones.

explanation.text:
Scenario: T1 (ts=10, older) wants lock held by T2 (ts=20, younger)

  Wait-Die:
    T1 older than T2 → T1 WAITS
    (if T2 had wanted T1's lock: T2 younger → T2 DIES)

  Wound-Wait:
    T1 older than T2 → T1 WOUNDS T2 (T2 aborts)
    (if T2 had wanted T1's lock: T2 younger → T2 WAITS)

Key property: neither protocol can form a cycle.
  Wait-Die: edges only go from older to younger → no cycle possible.
  Wound-Wait: edges only go from younger to older → no cycle possible.

runs.text: Both protocols guarantee deadlock-freedom because all wait edges point in one direction in the timestamp ordering: a cycle would require at least one edge pointing "backward", which neither protocol allows.

Wait-Die tends to abort more transactions (younger dies eagerly). Wound-Wait tends to abort younger transactions less often on the waiting side but forces preemptions. Most production databases use detection rather than avoidance because avoidance aborts transactions preventively even when no deadlock would have actually occurred.

Deadlock avoidance uses transaction timestamps to prevent cycles from forming. In wait-die, younger transactions die rather than wait for older ones. In wound-wait, older transactions kill younger ones rather than wait. Either way, all wait edges flow in one direction in the timestamp ordering, so a cycle is impossible.

cards.title: MVCC Version Chains — The Data Structure
cards.teaser: Multi-Version Concurrency Control keeps multiple versions of each row, linked in a chain. Each version records which transaction created it and which transaction deleted (or superseded) it. A reader walks the chain to find the version visible to its snapshot.

runs.text: In a single-version system, an UPDATE overwrites the old row. In MVCC, an UPDATE writes a
new version
of the row and marks the old version as superseded. The old version remains on the page (or in an undo log), forming a chain that historical readers can traverse.

explanation.text:
PostgreSQL heap tuple header (simplified):

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ t_xmin: 101   ← transaction that inserted this version      │
  │ t_xmax: 207   ← transaction that deleted/updated (0 = live) │
  │ t_ctid: (42,7)← pointer to newer version (self if current)  │
  │ data: { name='Alice', salary=85000 }                        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ↓  (t_ctid points to newer version)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ t_xmin: 207   ← written by T207                             │
  │ t_xmax: 0     ← currently live                              │
  │ t_ctid: self                                                │
  │ data: { name='Alice', salary=90000 }                        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

InnoDB stores old versions differently:
  - Current row lives in clustered index
  - Old versions live in the undo log segment
  - A "roll pointer" in the clustered index row links to the undo chain

runs.text: PostgreSQL stores all versions of a row in the heap (the main table file). This makes the version chain easy to follow (just follow
t_ctid

pointers) but causes table bloat: old versions occupy heap space until vacuumed. InnoDB stores the current version in the clustered index and old versions in a separate undo log, keeping the main index compact at the cost of undo log I/O for historical reads.

Oracle's implementation is the oldest commercial MVCC system (since Oracle 6, 1988). It stores undo data in rollback segments (now Automatic Undo Management segments). The version chain is reconstructed on demand: Oracle reads the current row from the data file, then applies undo records backward until it reaches the version visible to the query's SCN (System Change Number).

MVCC keeps multiple versions of each row. When a row is updated, the old version is not overwritten — it is kept and linked to the new version. Each version is stamped with the transaction that created it and the transaction that deleted it. Readers walk the chain to find the right version for their snapshot.

cards.title: Snapshot Isolation — Visibility Rules and the Engine View
cards.teaser: Under Snapshot Isolation, every transaction reads from a consistent snapshot taken at its start. The visibility rule is simple: a version is visible if its creating transaction committed before this transaction's snapshot, and its deleting transaction had not yet committed.

runs.text: When a transaction begins under Snapshot Isolation, the engine records a
snapshot
: the set of transaction IDs that were active (not yet committed) at that moment. The transaction then sees the world as it was at that instant.

explanation.text:
PostgreSQL visibility check (simplified):

A tuple version is visible to transaction T if:

  1. t_xmin is committed          (version was fully inserted)
  2. t_xmin < T.snapshot_xmin     (inserter committed before T's snapshot)
     OR t_xmin is in T.snapshot   (T itself created this version)
  3. t_xmax is 0                  (not deleted)
     OR t_xmax is not committed   (deleter had not committed at snapshot time)
     OR t_xmax >= T.snapshot_xmax (deleter started after T's snapshot)

Snapshot variables at T's start:
  xmin = lowest active XID        (all XIDs below this are committed)
  xmax = next XID to be assigned  (all XIDs above this are in the future)
  xip  = list of active XIDs between xmin and xmax

Oracle uses a System Change Number (SCN) instead of transaction ID lists:
  A version is visible if its commit SCN <= T's snapshot SCN.

runs.text: The power of SI is that reads never block writes and writes never block reads. Every reader sees a fully consistent snapshot without acquiring any read locks. This is why MVCC databases massively outperform lock-only systems under mixed read-write workloads.
SQL Server's
READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT

database option enables MVCC for Read Committed: instead of taking statement-level row locks, readers take a statement-level snapshot. This eliminates reader-writer blocking while preserving Read Committed semantics (each statement sees a fresh snapshot, not the transaction's start snapshot).

Snapshot Isolation works by giving each transaction a frozen view of the database at the moment it started. Every read goes through a visibility filter: only show versions whose creator had committed before my snapshot, and whose deleter had not yet committed. This means reads never need locks — they just check version metadata.

cards.title: Vacuum and Garbage Collection — Cleaning Dead Versions
cards.teaser: MVCC accumulates dead row versions — old versions that no transaction can ever need again. Without cleanup, tables grow without bound. PostgreSQL's VACUUM and InnoDB's purge thread are the engines' garbage collectors for dead MVCC versions.

runs.text: A row version becomes
dead
when its
t_xmax

(deleting transaction) has committed and no active snapshot can see it any more. The oldest snapshot horizon — the XID of the oldest active transaction — is the key threshold: any version superseded before that XID can be safely reclaimed.
PostgreSQL's VACUUM scans heap pages and removes dead tuple versions, freeing the space for reuse within the same page. Key behaviors:

items.text: VACUUM (non-blocking).
Reclaims dead tuple slots within pages. Does not return space to the OS — pages remain the same size, just with reusable slots. Runs concurrently with normal workload.
VACUUM FULL (blocking).
Rewrites the entire table to a new file, compacting it. Returns space to the OS. Acquires an exclusive lock — the table is unavailable during the operation.
autovacuum.
PostgreSQL's background daemon that runs VACUUM automatically based on configurable thresholds (default: vacuum when 20% of tuples are dead).
Transaction ID wraparound.

PostgreSQL uses 32-bit XIDs. After ~2 billion transactions, XIDs wrap around, making all future transactions appear "in the past" to old unfrozen tuples. VACUUM FREEZE prevents this by replacing old XIDs with the special FrozenTransactionId, making the tuple permanently visible. Failure to freeze causes catastrophic data loss.

runs.text: InnoDB's
purge thread

removes old undo log segments and cleans deleted index records. Because InnoDB stores old versions in the undo log (not in the heap), "purge" cleans undo segments rather than table pages. A long-running read transaction prevents purge from advancing — the undo log grows until that transaction completes. This is why analytics queries running against OLTP InnoDB databases can cause severe undo log bloat.

An idle transaction that holds an open snapshot blocks VACUUM (PostgreSQL) or undo purge (InnoDB). In high-write workloads, a forgotten long-running transaction is one of the most common causes of table bloat and performance degradation. Monitor pg_stat_activity and innodb_trx for long-running transactions.

MVCC keeps old row versions so live snapshots can read them. Once every snapshot that could ever see an old version is gone, that version is dead garbage. PostgreSQL's VACUUM sweeps heap pages and marks those slots reusable. InnoDB's purge thread cleans the undo log. Both are blocked by any transaction holding an old enough snapshot.

cards.title: SSI — Serializable Snapshot Isolation
cards.teaser: Serializable Snapshot Isolation (Cahill et al., 2008) extends Snapshot Isolation to full serializability by tracking read-write dependencies and aborting transactions that form a "dangerous structure" — a cycle in the dependency graph that would produce a non-serializable outcome.

runs.text: Snapshot Isolation is almost serializable. The gap — write skew and read-only anomalies — comes from a specific pattern in the dependency graph identified by Adya (1999) and exploited by Cahill, Röhm, and Fekete (2008) in their VLDB paper "Serializable Isolation for Snapshot Databases".
Cahill's key insight: every non-serializable SI execution contains a
dangerous structure

: two consecutive rw-anti-dependency edges (read-write conflicts) forming a pivot in the serialization graph. Concretely: T1 reads data written by T2, and T2 reads data written by T3, and T3 reads data that conflicts with T1's reads — the three form a cycle.

explanation.text:
Dangerous structure (the pivot pattern):

  T1 ──rw──► T2 ──rw──► T3
   ▲                     │
   └──────── rw ─────────┘   ← this third edge creates the cycle

SSI detects this by tracking:
  - SIREAD locks: which rows/predicates each transaction has read
  - Outgoing rw-conflicts: T_i has a row that T_j later reads and T_i has updated
  - Incoming rw-conflicts: T_j has read a row that T_i later updated

When a transaction gains BOTH an incoming AND an outgoing rw-conflict,
it sits at the pivot of a dangerous structure → abort the pivot transaction.

PostgreSQL implementation (pg 9.1+):
  - SIREAD locks are lightweight (stored in a separate SIREAD lock table)
  - Committed transactions' conflict data is kept briefly to catch late-arriving pivots
  - Aborts the pivot with error: ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write
    dependencies among transactions (SQLSTATE 40001)

runs.text: The on-call doctor scenario (card 5) under SSI: T1 reads the doctor count and updates Alice; T2 reads the same count and updates Bob. T1 has a rw-conflict with T2 (T2 wrote after T1 read), and T2 has a rw-conflict with T1 (T1 wrote after T2 read). Both sit at pivots — SSI aborts one of them.

SSI overhead is low on the happy path: no extra locks on the write path, only lightweight SIREAD locks on reads. PostgreSQL benchmarks show SSI overhead of 4–8% on TPC-C vs plain SI — dramatically lower than the 2x+ overhead of S2PL with predicate locks. This makes SSI the most practical path to serializable isolation in MVCC systems.

SSI was integrated into PostgreSQL by Kevin Grittner and Dan Ports in 2011 (pg 9.1). It was the first widely-deployed production implementation of Cahill et al.'s algorithm. Ports and Grittner published a follow-up paper at VLDB 2012 showing that SSI's overhead in production workloads was much lower than theoretically expected, validating it as a practical replacement for S2PL.

SSI makes Snapshot Isolation fully serializable by watching for a specific dangerous pattern: two consecutive read-write conflicts that form a cycle. When a transaction ends up at the pivot of that cycle, SSI aborts it. On the happy path — no cycles — there is almost no overhead compared to ordinary SI, which is what makes SSI practical.
